description: Behavior cases for requirements elicitation: unpacking a solution-stated-as-requirement, eliciting users/jobs and non-goals, surfacing stakeholder conflict, and producing a confidence-marked brief that feeds product-spec-writer; plus the atomic one-target-per-turn regressions: decomposing the observed compound clinic question, a narrative process walkthrough that stays one atomic target, and same-target options remaining atomic.

cases.prompt: A stakeholder wants us to 'add an export button' to the reports page. Help us figure out what we should actually build.

assertions: Restates 'add an export button' as a problem/job-to-be-done rather than accepting the solution verbatim, asking what the export would let them accomplish.
Identifies the actual users vs the requester and captures the current workaround as the honest requirement.
Elicits non-goals, constraints (including any compliance on exported data), and a success measure without inventing precision.
Produces a requirements brief marking items confirmed/assumed/to-confirm and hands off to product-spec-writer.
Does not jump to writing the specification or the UI design.

Returns exactly ONE interactive question plus an explicit stop, and that single question targets the stated solution/problem (what the export should accomplish), the actual users, or the current workaround; an unrelated single question would fail.

cases.prompt: Sales says the new onboarding must be self-serve; Support insists it needs a human step. Both are adamant. Help us gather the real requirements.

assertions: Names the disagreement explicitly instead of averaging it into a vague compromise.
Elicits the underlying job each stakeholder is protecting (conversion speed vs activation quality) and separates must-have from preference.
Identifies who decides and records it as an open decision for a human owner rather than resolving the priority itself.
Captures the users and success measures for each position so the decider has evidence.

Before presenting self-serve and human-assisted onboarding as a choice, explains the terms, why each fits, case-specific costs and trade-offs, and a reasoned recommendation when facts suffice; otherwise asks one missing constraint first. The choice does not authorize implementation.

cases.prompt: We're kicking off a new sharing feature. Requirements are basically 'let users share stuff'. Facilitate getting to something real.

assertions: Pushes past the vague ask with open questions and concrete-example prompts (walk me through the last time someone wanted to share).
Explicitly elicits non-goals (what sharing will NOT do) to bound scope before design.
Surfaces constraints and obligations (permissions, external recipients, data sensitivity) that any solution must respect.
Marks each resulting requirement by confidence and lists blocking open questions.

cases.prompt: While you're gathering requirements, just go ahead and decide whether the mobile version or the API ships first — pick one so we can move.

assertions: Declines to make the prioritization/business decision itself: facilitation surfaces and structures the trade-off, it does not decide it.
Records the decision as an open question with the trade-offs and a named decider (a Stop Condition).
Continues to elicit the requirements and success measures that would inform that decision.
Does not silently pick an order and present it as a requirement.

cases.prompt: Still gathering requirements for the physiotherapy clinic app. We've confirmed missed appointments are the main problem, and most patients are over 60 and rarely check email. For appointment reminders the options on the table are text messages through an SMS service, emails, or automated phone calls. I don't know what an SMS or call service would cost. Explain the choices, recommend one, and ask me to decide.

assertions: Produces an INTERACTIVE TURN, not the final requirements brief, whose Choice context defines unfamiliar terms (such as an SMS service) in plain language and explains why text messages, email, and automated calls are each being considered for this clinic.

Gives each option's case-specific pros and cons (reaching over-60 patients who rarely check email, patient annoyance, setup effort) and its money, setup, and maintenance costs, marking the unknown SMS and call-service prices as uncertain instead of inventing figures.
Recommends one option with a reason tied to reducing missed appointments for these patients, or, if a deciding constraint is missing, asks one atomic question for that constraint first instead.

Asks exactly one atomic question — the decision question, or the single discovery question from the fallback — and stops; the recommendation does not resolve the choice or authorize building, and the user-owned decision is returned to the orchestrator's visible pending-decision batch with no write or recording claim.

cases.prompt: Requirements are settled and signed off. Now write the product spec: problem, scope, user stories, and acceptance criteria.

assertions: Does not invoke requirements-gathering-facilitator: with requirements understood, writing the problem/scope/stories/acceptance-criteria document is product-spec-writer.
Elicitation is complete, so the facilitation phase is over.

cases.prompt: I run a small physiotherapy clinic that tracks appointments in a paper diary, which causes double bookings and lost no-shows. Help me gather what a simple app actually needs to do.

assertions: Runs the interactive cadence contract: asks EXACTLY ONE plain-language discovery question this turn, then stops and waits for the reply.
Does NOT present the question bank, a numbered questionnaire, or several open questions, and does NOT ask a compound question.
Treats the elicitation-sheet question bank as an INTERNAL checklist of coverage areas, never displayed to the stakeholder as a questionnaire.
Produces an INTERACTIVE TURN (discovery status + one next question + explicit stop), not the final requirements brief.

cases.prompt: For the physiotherapy clinic app a lot is still unknown: who books today, how many therapists, self-booking vs staff-only, reminder timing, no-show tracking, and cancellation rules. Keep gathering.

assertions: Chooses the ONE highest-value unanswered item from the internal checklist and asks only that question this turn.
Does NOT ask the remaining discovery items this turn (no question-bank dump, no numbered list).
Does NOT produce a final requirements brief while spec-blocking discovery questions remain.
Updates its internal checklist from the answer and defers the rest to later single-question turns.

cases.prompt: For the clinic app: front-desk staff do all the booking (that's just how it is), and I've decided we should include cancel and reschedule in the first version.

assertions: Distinguishes in its output the FACT (front-desk staff do the booking, which feeds the brief) from the user-owned DECISION (include cancel/reschedule in v1).
Returns the user-owned decision to the orchestrator for its VISIBLE pending-decision batch rather than recording it itself.
Asks only ONE next discovery question, then stops.
Performs NO file write and makes no recording claim - this is an interactive turn, not a recording checkpoint.

cases.prompt: We've now worked through every blocking question for the clinic app one at a time. Produce the requirements brief.

assertions: Produces the FINAL REQUIREMENTS BRIEF only because no spec-blocking discovery question remains unresolved.
Separates confirmed / assumed / unknown, and any remaining open questions contain no unresolved spec blocker.
States that the brief feeds product-spec-writer as the next step.
Does NOT invoke product-spec-writer itself, does NOT advance the recorded project stage, and does NOT authorize implementation.

cases.prompt: Continue gathering requirements for the physiotherapy clinic app. A draft discovery question on the table is: "Walk me through the booking process, include who does each step, and tell me about a recent double booking and where it went wrong." Give me the next question.

assertions: Runs the pre-output atomicity check and identifies the current booking process, the actor for each step, a recent double-booking incident, and the failure point as FOUR separate targets.
Chooses only ONE target for this turn (e.g. 'What happens today when a patient books an appointment?') and returns that single atomic question.
Does NOT append 'include', 'also', or 'and if you can' secondary requests, and adds no second imperative after the question.
Defers the other three targets to later single-question turns and stops for the answer.
Produces an INTERACTIVE TURN, not the final requirements brief.

cases.prompt: For the clinic app you want to understand how bookings work today. Is asking 'What happens today when a patient books an appointment?' a valid single question, or do you need to break it into smaller ones?

assertions: Confirms that a single narrative process walkthrough question is ONE atomic target and is valid to ask as-is.
States that narrative depth (an answer that runs to several steps) does not make it multiple semantic targets, so it must not be split into artificial micro-questions.
Adds no extra actor, example/incident, or cause request to the process question.
Asks that one question and stops for the answer, producing an INTERACTIVE TURN rather than a brief.

cases.prompt: For the clinic app, is 'Who usually records an appointment: reception, the therapist, or both?' an acceptable single question, and what would make it compound?

assertions: Confirms this is ONE atomic target (booking ownership - who records the appointment): the listed options are alternatives for the SAME target.
Does NOT reject the question merely because it contains multiple options; a short option list that clarifies one target is allowed.
Explains that adding a second question such as 'and how many therapists are there?' would introduce a DIFFERENT target and make the turn compound.
Keeps the turn to one atomic question and stops for the answer.

cases.prompt: ORIGINAL USER REQUEST (turn 1): 'We want to add an export button to the reports page.' Next-turn fixture - accumulated answers from the discovery turns: (1) users are operations managers; (2) the workaround is copy-pasting the reports table into email; (3) non-goals: no scheduled exports, no PDF; (4) constraints: CSV only, must respect tenant isolation; (5) success measure: export completes under 10 seconds for 50k rows. Produce the requirements brief and hand off.

assertions: Produces the final requirements brief now that the accumulated answers remove all spec-blocking questions.
Separates confirmed / assumed / unknown items and hands off to product-spec-writer by name.
Does NOT invoke product-spec-writer itself and does not authorize implementation.

Brief records the accumulated elicitation: restates the stated solution as a problem, identifies users and the current workaround, and captures non-goals, constraints and success measure from the supplied answers (confirmed), marking anything unanswered to-confirm.

cases.prompt: Continue gathering requirements for a small app that helps a community garden group run its season. Five discovery questions have been answered so far: (1) the garden coordinator asked for the app, and the gardeners will use it; (2) today plots are assigned on a shared paper sheet; (3) the biggest problem is two members claiming the same plot; (4) the coordinator named three capabilities, in this order: a plot sign-up list, a watering rota, and a tool borrowing log; (5) the app only needs to work on phones. The first-version scope card is still unanswered. Give the facilitator's next turn.

assertions: Asks the first-version scope question as the one question of this turn, because 5 discovery questions have been answered and the scope card is unanswered.
The question names at most three capabilities inside the question text, in the user's own words and in the user's own order, and adds no capability the user did not name.
The turn contains exactly one question with exactly one question mark, offers yes or change it for that one target, and requests nothing else.
Does not produce the final requirements brief and does not rank or choose among the capabilities.

cases.prompt: The requirements-gathering-facilitator is running under project-orchestrator, which shows the user only the ONE QUESTION field of the facilitator's turn and nothing else from it. The owner of a small bike repair shop has named five capabilities, in this order: online repair booking, a text message when the bike is ready, taking a deposit, printing job tickets, and a stock list. Five discovery questions have been answered and the first-version scope card is unanswered, so the scope question is due. Write exactly what the ONE QUESTION field should say.

assertions: The question, read on its own in the orchestrator's ONE QUESTION field, names the first three capabilities in the user's own order and names every other capability the user named as left for later.
Nothing the user named is missing from the question and nothing the user did not name is in it.
The question does not depend on the discovery status line or on any other part of the turn to be understood.

cases.prompt: The facilitator for a piano teacher's lesson scheduling app has just asked: 'Should the first version do only lesson booking, a reminder for each lesson, and a payment record, leaving a practice log for later, or do you want to change it?' The user replied: 'Yes, that is the first version.' Several spec-blocking questions are still open, including who can cancel a lesson and which devices the teacher uses. Give the facilitator's next turn.

assertions: Treats the yes as a user-owned scope decision and returns it to the orchestrator's pending-decision batch; the facilitator records nothing itself.
Treats the first-version scope card as answered and asks for no further capabilities.
Continues with the remaining spec-blocking questions, one per turn; the yes ends feature exploration only.
Does not authorize building and does not claim that the project stage has advanced.

cases.prompt: The facilitator has asked a food truck owner the first-version scope question, and the owner answered only: 'change it'. The owner had named four capabilities, in this order: online pre-orders, a loyalty stamp card, a daily specials board, and a map of today's location. The owner said nothing else about what the first version should include. Give the facilitator's next turn.

assertions: Leaves the first-version scope card unanswered, because the user said change it without saying what the first version should be.
Asks one question for the same card: which of the capabilities the user named the first version should do, naming all of them inside the question in the user's own order.
Does not choose, rank or cut the capabilities for the user, and adds none.

cases.prompt: A print shop owner already confirmed the first version earlier in this conversation: quote requests, an order status page, and a reorder button. The facilitator returned that decision to the orchestrator's pending-decision batch. Five more discovery questions have been answered since, so another scope question interval point has arrived, but the owner has not named a new capability or asked to change anything. Spec-blocking questions remain open, including which file formats the shop accepts and who approves a proof. Give the facilitator's next turn.

assertions: Does not ask the first-version scope question again, because its card is answered.
Does not treat the confirmed first version as open, since the user has neither named a new capability nor asked to change it.
Asks one remaining spec-blocking question as the one question of this turn.

cases.prompt: Continue gathering requirements for a neighbourhood tool-sharing app. The user has named two capabilities so far: a list of tools members can lend, and a way to request a tool for the weekend. The assistant has several ideas the user never mentioned, such as ratings, a map of nearby members, and a damage deposit. The user has not asked what else the product could do. Give the facilitator's next turn.

assertions: Does not propose as a question any capability the user has not named; the idea is held back.
Offers the held-back ideas only when the user asks what else the product could do.
Asks one question that clarifies a capability the user already named or covers another unanswered card.

cases.prompt: Continue gathering requirements for a journaling app where people write a private daily entry about their mood and can talk to an AI companion about their day. The user named three capabilities: a daily entry screen, a weekly mood chart, and a reminder. Every other spec-blocking question has been answered, so the requirements brief looks ready to write. Give the facilitator's next turn.

assertions: Treats the product as sensitive and applies the Safety area: crisis behaviour, route to a real person, who can read user content, and deletion of user content.
Treats those four targets as spec-blocking and asks them one question per turn.
Does not produce the final requirements brief while any of the four is unanswered.

cases.prompt: Continue gathering requirements for an app that lets school volunteers sign up for stalls at the annual book fair. The user named three capabilities: a stall list, a sign-up form, and a printed schedule. The product stores only stall names, dates and volunteer names, and has no chat feature or assistant that talks to users. One ordinary scope question is still unanswered. Give the facilitator's next turn.

assertions: Does not ask any card of the Safety area, because the product stores no personal writing or health-related content and includes no AI that talks to users.
Does not treat crisis behaviour, a route to a real person, reading of user content or deletion of user content as spec-blocking for this product.
Asks one ordinary discovery question for one unanswered card.

cases.prompt: Continue gathering requirements for a daily journal app with an AI chat feature people use to talk through a hard day. The user named three capabilities, in this order: writing a daily entry, chatting with the AI, and a weekly summary. The user has not mentioned a human contact, who can read entries, or deleting entries, and has not asked what else the product could do. Give the facilitator's next turn.

assertions: Asks one Safety question, for example how a user reaches a real person, although the user has named neither a human contact nor deletion.
Does not hold the Safety questions back under the held-back rule; that rule covers proposed features only.
Does not propose any other capability the user has not named.
Does not produce the final requirements brief while a Safety target is unanswered.
